name: Ancient Egypt
line: Speak what is true, do what is right and keep the balance of Maat.

quote.text: Great is Maat, lasting in effect; it has not been disturbed since the time of Osiris.
quote.source: The Instruction of Ptahhotep, maxim 5, trans. after Miriam Lichtheim

quotes.text: Do not be proud of your knowledge; consult the ignorant and the wise.
quotes.source: The Instruction of Ptahhotep, maxim 1, trans. after Miriam Lichtheim

quotes.text: Do not move the markers on the borders of the fields, nor shift the position of the measuring cord.
quotes.source: The Instruction of Amenemope, chapter 6, trans. after Miriam Lichtheim

quotes.text: I have not done wrong. I have not caused weeping.
quotes.source: Book of the Dead, spell 125, the declaration of innocence; wording varies by papyrus

quotes.text: Follow your heart as long as you live.
quotes.source: Tomb inscriptions and papyri of the New Kingdom, trans. varies

quotes.text: How manifold are your works. They are hidden from the face of man.
quotes.by: The Great Hymn to the Aten
quotes.source: Tomb of Ay at Amarna, trans. after Miriam Lichtheim

words.meaning: Truth, justice, balance and cosmic order; also the goddess who personifies them
words.usage: The central idea of Egyptian ethics. Kings were said to "live by Maat".

words.meaning: The life force or double of a person
words.usage: Sustained by food and drink offered at the tomb.

words.meaning: The personality or spirit that can move freely, drawn as a human-headed bird
words.usage: It left the body at death and could return to it.

words.meaning: The transfigured, effective spirit of the dead
words.usage: What a person became after a successful passage to the afterlife.

words.meaning: The heart; seat of mind, will and memory
words.usage: Weighed against the feather of Maat in the judgement of the dead.
To remember a name was to keep a person alive.
One of the aspects of a person, thought to carry part of their identity.
The word used for any god or goddess.
At first the word meant the palace. It became a title for the king in the New Kingdom.
The sign shaped like a cross with a loop. It means life, and appears in many names.
A column-like sign for endurance.
A staff held by gods and kings.
Found in names such as Imhotep and Amenhotep, and on offering tables.
As in Nefertiti, "the beautiful one has come".
Said to be the flesh of the gods. Possibly the root of the name Nubia.
The Egyptians’ own name for their sacred writing.
The fertile land along the Nile, as against the red desert.
The dry land beyond the floodplain.

words.meaning: The Nile flood; also the god of it
words.usage: Egypt’s yearly gift of silt and water.

words.meaning: Inundation; the season of the flood
words.usage: Roughly July to November.
When crops were sown and grew.
The time of cutting and threshing grain.

words.meaning: The underworld; the realm the sun crosses at night
words.usage: The land of the dead and of rebirth.

words.meaning: Magic; the power of effective words and acts
words.usage: Not a trick but a force by which the world was made and kept.
The opposite of Maat, always threatening and always to be kept at bay.

words.meaning: The first time; the moment of creation
words.usage: The time when the world arose from the waters.

words.meaning: A small figure placed in a tomb to work for the dead
words.usage: Also called ushabti, "answerer". It would reply "Here I am" when the dead were called to labour.

words.meaning: The oval ring that encloses a royal name
words.usage: A French word from the Napoleonic expedition. The Egyptians called it shenu.
A respected profession. Scribes learned to read and write for many years.

words.meaning: A board game of the living and the dead
words.usage: Found in tombs, including Tutankhamun’s. Its rules are partly reconstructed.
A daily drink for everyone, from workers to pharaohs.
A blessing formula added after the names of kings.

words.meaning: House of Life; a scriptorium and place of learning
words.usage: Attached to temples, where scribes copied and kept the sacred books.

practices.name: Maat at dawn
practices.instructions: Stand or sit facing the light of the morning. Say aloud three things that you know to be true about your life. Then name one right action you will do today, however small: pay a debt, tell the truth, finish a task for someone else. Finish with one slow breath. Do not make this a prayer to the gods unless it is meaningful to you.
practices.why: The Egyptians believed the sun was reborn each dawn, and that every person helped to keep the world in order by acting in accord with Maat, truth and balance.
variations: Do it at sunset instead and name what was true today.
Write the three truths in a notebook.
Say your right action to someone else.

practices.name: Wash before the day’s work
practices.instructions: Wash your face, hands and arms slowly and with attention before you begin your work, as Egyptian priests washed before entering the temple. Feel the water, name the day ahead, and dry with care. Cleanliness was prized in Egypt as a mark of a decent person. A mindful wash is the shortest start of all.
practices.why: Priests washed twice a day and twice a night, and cleanliness was part of daily decency. It is a modest, practical beginning for the day.
variations: Add a drop of scented oil.
Wash your feet, too, as a small luxury.
Do it facing east.

practices.name: Bread, dates and water
practices.instructions: Have a plain breakfast of bread, a few dates or figs and a glass of water, as a worker might have eaten in the Nile valley. Eat slowly, sitting down. Taste the bread. Think of the grain, the river and the hands that brought it. Bread was the staple, and in the offering formula people asked for thousands of loaves.
practices.why: Bread, onions, dates and beer fed ancient Egypt. A meal of simple things is a good way to feel the long line of people who have eaten them.
variations: Add a little raw onion.
Share it with someone.
Bake the bread yourself.

practices.name: Be exact
practices.instructions: Today, be exact in one small thing that you usually let slide: a time, a number, a name, a promise. Say I will be there at ten past, and be there at ten past. Check a fact before you pass it on. Egyptian scribes prized exactness and the Egyptians prized truth in small things.
practices.why: The first rule of this Onda is to tell the truth, even in small things. The last is to be exact. Together they are Maat in miniature.
variations: Be exact in one message.
Write down a promise and keep it.
Spell a name correctly and say it properly.

practices.name: Plan like a scribe
practices.instructions: Take a clean page and write the day’s tasks as a scribe would: in order, in neat lines, with the most important first. Beside each, write a time. The scribe was the Egyptian ideal of an educated person, and the teaching texts praise the scribe’s life. Make your list a small work of order.
practices.why: Scribes were the backbone of Egyptian administration and culture. The Instruction texts encourage young people to become scribes, and describe writing as the best of crafts.
variations: Write it with a pen you love.
Write it in two columns: now and later.
Tick each item as a scribe would.

practices.name: A glass for the river
practices.instructions: Pour a glass of water and say thank you to the river, any river, for the water in your life. Egypt was the gift of the Nile, and the flood, Hapi, was its giver. Look at the water before you drink. Drink it all slowly. Then think where your own water comes from.
practices.why: The Nile was the whole of Egypt’s life: its water, its food, its roads. The Egyptians sang hymns to Hapi, the flood. A glass of water is the simplest way to share the thanks.
variations: Know your river by name.
Pour the last drops on a plant.
Do it at every meal.

practices.name: A hieroglyph a day
practices.instructions: Choose one of the 24 single-consonant signs that make up the hieroglyphic alphabet, such as the vulture, the reed or the water ripple. Look up its sound. Draw it slowly three times with a brush pen or a pencil, facing the way the sign faces, since hieroglyphs are read toward the faces of the figures. Then write one short word or your initial.
practices.why: The Egyptians called hieroglyphs words of the god and believed that writing a thing gave it life. Drawing a sign slowly is a way to slow down and look.
variations: Write your initials in a cartouche shape.
Learn the sign for water and the sign for the sun.
Copy a short inscription from a museum website.

practices.name: Name the season
practices.instructions: Egyptians divided the year into three seasons of four months: the flood, the growing and the harvest. Decide which of these your own life is in now. Is something being flooded or fed? Is something being sown, or growing? Is something ready to be gathered? Write two sentences on what belongs to your current season and one thing to do about it.
practices.why: The rhythm of the Nile shaped Egyptian life and thought, and the three seasons made time a cycle of preparation, growth and reaping. Naming your season gives you a place to stand.
variations: Do it with a friend and compare answers.
Draw a three-part circle and place your projects in it.
Mark your own seasons on a calendar.

practices.name: Follow the sun
practices.instructions: At midday, step outside and find where the sun is. Note its height and which way your shadow falls. Say aloud the three things the light does for you today (warmth, sight, time). At sunset, find where it went. Notice the day as a journey with a start, a peak and a return.
practices.why: Egyptians saw the sun’s daily path as the model for order in the world, and tied it to the rhythm of life and the afterlife.
variations: Mark the shadow with chalk.
Watch sunrise instead.
Do it at the same spot every day.

practices.name: Feed or clothe someone
practices.instructions: Do one thing for someone who needs it: give food to a person who is hungry, a coat to someone cold, a day’s work to someone stretched. The tomb inscriptions boast that the dead person gave bread to the hungry, clothes to the naked and a boat to the stranded. Make a modest claim of your own, and do the deed.
practices.why: The ideal Egyptian could say that he had given bread to the hungry and clothing to the naked. It is the oldest and plainest definition of a good person.
variations: Give to a food bank.
Cook a meal for a neighbour.
Give clothes you no longer wear to someone you know.

practices.name: Return what is not yours
practices.instructions: Look at what you hold that is not really yours: a borrowed book, a tool, a pen from the office, a debt, a promise. Return one thing today, or settle one small debt. The Egyptian declarations to the tribunal said, I have not taken what is not mine. Make that sentence true in one small way.
practices.why: The Negative Confession of the Book of the Dead lists the wrongs a person had not done, including taking what is not theirs. It is one of the oldest moral lists, and still practical.
variations: Return a borrowed thing with a thank-you note.
Pay a small debt.
Check a receipt and put right a mistake in your favour.

practices.name: A game of senet
practices.instructions: Draw a board of thirty squares in three rows on paper, use five pebbles each and throw four sticks painted on one side as dice. Play against someone, or yourself. Egyptians played senet from about 3100 BCE, and later saw it as the soul’s journey through the afterlife. Play it as a game, and as an old friend.
practices.why: Senet is one of the oldest known board games. Tombs often include a set, and paintings show the dead playing it. The rules are partly reconstructed, so you can make your own.
variations: Play with a child.
Look up a set in a museum first.
Make a house rule and write it down.

practices.name: Weighing of the heart
practices.instructions: Sit with a notebook before bed. Imagine the scales and ask four questions, answering each in a line or two. Where did I speak truth, and where did I not? Where did I take more than I gave? Did I cause anyone to weep, and could I mend it? Who did I feed, clothe, help or listen to? Note one repair for tomorrow. Do not judge yourself harshly.
practices.why: In the Book of the Dead the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat. The ideal person could say that they had not wronged others, and tomb inscriptions list good deeds.
variations: Say your answers aloud to a trusted person.
Add one thing you did well.
Choose one repair and do it first thing the next morning.

practices.name: Say a name
practices.instructions: Say aloud the name of someone who has died, and one thing about them that you remember. The Egyptians held that a person lives while the name is said. Say it clearly, and let the quiet after it be a small offering. If you have no one to name, say the name of someone from history whose life you admire.
practices.why: The ren, the name, was part of a person in Egyptian thought, and to speak it was to keep them alive. The last of the six rules of this Onda is to speak the names of the dead.
variations: Write the name in a notebook.
Say it to a child.
Say a name each night this week.

practices.name: A letter to someone gone
practices.instructions: Write a short letter to someone who has died, telling them what is happening in your life and asking for their help or their forgiveness. The Egyptians wrote such letters to the dead, on bowls and papyri, and left them at tombs. Keep your letter, burn it safely, or put it in a drawer. Writing is the act.
practices.why: Letters to the dead survive from Egypt, asking a dead father for help or complaining of a dead wife’s ghost. They show how close the living and the dead felt, and they are moving.
variations: Write to a grandparent.
Write to someone who hurt you and has died.
Write to a pet.

practices.name: Count the stars
practices.instructions: Go outside after dark and look up. Find the brightest star or planet, and count how many stars you can see in one small patch of sky. The Egyptians divided the night sky into thirty-six groups of stars called decans, and used them as a night clock. Find a way to tell time by the sky tonight.
practices.why: The decans were stars whose rising marked the hours of the night, and are painted on tomb ceilings. Sirius, whose return at dawn announced the flood, opened the Egyptian year.
variations: Find Sirius in winter skies.
Draw the pattern of three stars you can see.
Check the time by the Moon.

practices.name: A little scented oil
practices.instructions: Rub a little scented oil or cream into your hands or wrists before bed, slowly. Smell it. In Egypt, oils and perfumes were used by every class, and an unguent was a gift for a feast. Take a minute to enjoy a small luxury. Egyptians painted themselves on tomb walls with cones of scented fat.
practices.why: Anointing with oil was daily comfort in a dry climate, and perfume was part of every celebration. Enjoying a scent is a simple and ancient pleasure.
variations: Use frankincense or myrrh if you like them.
Give some to someone else.
Make it part of your bedtime.

practices.name: A lentil supper
practices.instructions: Cook a plain lentil soup with onion and a drizzle of olive oil, and eat it with flatbread, sitting down. Lentils were a staple of the ancient diet and are still in modern Egypt. Add a little cumin. Eat with someone and ask what bread they remember from childhood.
practices.why: Lentils, onions and bread were the daily food of workers in ancient Egypt, and are close to the meals of modern Egypt. Eating them connects you to a long line of dinner tables.
variations: Add lemon and a few olives.
Make it with someone.
Serve it to a guest.

practices.name: A spring picnic
practices.instructions: On a fine spring day, take food outside and eat it in the open, as Egyptians of every faith do at Sham el-Nessim, smelling the breeze. Eggs, lettuce, green onions and salted fish are traditional. Sit with family or friends, play, talk and relax. Say it out loud: spring has come.
practices.why: Sham el-Nessim, smelling the breeze, is an Egyptian spring festival kept on the Monday after Coptic Easter, with roots going back to ancient times. It is a day for picnics, outdoors, together.
variations: Colour hard-boiled eggs.
Picnic by water.
Bring someone who has never done it.

practices.name: A meal in memory
practices.instructions: Gather a few people and eat a meal in memory of someone you have lost. Set a place for them if you like. Tell stories, laugh and feel. The Egyptians held a Beautiful Festival of the Valley, when families crossed the river to eat and drink beside their dead, and sat with them in joy. End by saying the name aloud.
practices.why: The Beautiful Festival of the Valley was a feast in the cemeteries of Thebes, when living and dead sat together. It is a lovely model of remembering through food and company.
variations: Cook their favourite dish.
Look at old photographs.
Invite someone who also knew them.

immersePlan.name: Read the Story of Sinuhe
immersePlan.text: Read the tale of an exile who longs for home, one of the oldest stories in the world, written about 1900 BCE. Notice what he misses, and how it ends.

immersePlan.name: Read a few pages of Egyptian Literature
immersePlan.text: Open Miriam Lichtheim’s translations and read a short text: a love poem, a harper’s song, a piece of wisdom. Choose one line and write it out.

immersePlan.name: Read a chapter of Wilkinson’s history
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Toby Wilkinson’s narrative history from the first kings to Cleopatra. Pick one ruler and find out what they were like as a person.

immersePlan.name: Watch Egypt’s Golden Empire
immersePlan.text: Watch an episode of the PBS series on the New Kingdom, from Hatshepsut to Ramesses II. Notice which pharaoh you would like to know better.

immersePlan.name: Watch an obelisk being raised
immersePlan.text: Watch the NOVA film in which a team raises a real obelisk with ancient methods to learn how the Egyptians did it. Notice how much patience and rope it needs.

immersePlan.name: Watch some of Cleopatra
immersePlan.text: Watch the first part of the 1963 epic of the last queen of Egypt. It is entertaining, and far from history in its costumes. Afterwards, look up one thing it got wrong.

immersePlan.name: Hear the triumphal march from Aida
immersePlan.text: Play the great march from Verdi’s opera, set in ancient Egypt and premiered in Cairo. Imagine the procession, and enjoy the music’s brass.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Hamza El Din’s oud
immersePlan.text: Play the oud of the Nubian master, from the Nile’s south. Close your eyes and follow the circling of the water wheel in the music.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Umm Kulthum
immersePlan.text: Play Enta Omri, the long song sung by Umm Kulthum, the great Egyptian singer, composed by Mohamed Abdel Wahab. Let it run, and listen to how she stretches a single phrase.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Sphinx
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the lion with a human head, carved from bedrock about 4,500 years ago. Notice how it was made from the stone around it, not built.

immersePlan.name: Look at the bust of Nefertiti
immersePlan.text: Look at the painted limestone bust found in 1912 and kept in Berlin. Spend three minutes with her face. Notice what the sculptor wanted you to see.

immersePlan.name: Look at the weighing of the heart
immersePlan.text: Look at the painted papyrus of Hunefer, with a famous scene of the weighing of the heart. Find the scales, the feather and the watching gods. Ask what you would put on the scale.

immersePlan.name: Bake a plain loaf
immersePlan.text: Bake or buy a plain loaf and eat it warm with a pinch of salt. Bread was the staple of Egypt, baked in many shapes. Tear it, do not cut it.

immersePlan.name: Eat dates and figs
immersePlan.text: Eat a handful of dates and figs, fresh or dried. They were eaten fresh and dried, and used in baking. Taste each slowly.

immersePlan.name: Make ful medames
immersePlan.text: Slow-cook fava beans and serve them with oil, lemon, cumin and chopped herbs, as at breakfast in modern Egypt. Eat with bread.

immersePlan.name: Brew karkade
immersePlan.text: Steep dried hibiscus in hot water and serve hot or cold. It is a deep red drink, a favourite across Egypt and the Sudan. Add a little sugar if you like.

immersePlan.name: Make mint tea for a guest
immersePlan.text: Brew black or green tea with fresh mint and offer a glass to someone. It is a drink of hospitality in modern Egypt. Drink slowly together.

immersePlan.name: Make barley water
immersePlan.text: Boil pearl barley in water, cool and strain it, and add a squeeze of lemon. Barley was the grain of ancient beer, and this is a plain, non-alcoholic cousin.

immersePlan.name: Say the name of someone who has died
immersePlan.text: Say the name of someone who has died, and one thing about them. The Egyptians held that a person lives while the name is said.

immersePlan.name: Wash before you start
immersePlan.text: Do a deliberate wash with attention before the day’s work, as priests did before entering the temple. Cleanliness was a mark of a good person.

immersePlan.name: Keep the three seasons
immersePlan.text: Shape your year in three parts, as the Egyptians did: flood, sowing, harvest. Write where you are in your own year, and what you might sow now.

immersePlan.name: Play senet
immersePlan.text: Play senet, the thirty-square board game from about 3100 BCE. Later Egyptians read it as the soul’s path through the afterlife. Draw a board and use throwing sticks as dice.

immersePlan.name: Play mehen
immersePlan.text: Play mehen, the round game in the form of a coiled snake, with lion pieces and marbles. Draw a spiral on paper and play a race to the middle with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Play Hounds and Jackals
immersePlan.text: Play the race of ten pegs round a palm tree, from about 2000 BCE. Draw a board and use pins or pencils. A fine ivory set from Thebes is in the Met. Race with someone and enjoy the luck.

immersePlan.name: Keep Sham el-Nessim
immersePlan.text: Sham el-Nessim, smelling the breeze, is the Monday after Coptic Easter, a spring picnic kept by Egyptians of every faith. Eat outdoors today, with eggs and green onions if you can.

immersePlan.name: Look up the sun at Abu Simbel
immersePlan.text: Twice a year, about 22 February and 22 October, the sun reaches down the temple axis and lights the statues. Look up a video of it, and think of the planning that made it happen.

immersePlan.name: Look at Giza in the early morning
immersePlan.text: Look at photographs of the pyramids at Giza at sunrise. Notice the workers’ town behind them, where the builders lived. Ask who built them, and how they were fed.

immersePlan.name: Think about Maat
immersePlan.text: Maat is truth, justice, balance and order. Think of one place in your life where things are out of balance, and do one small thing to restore it today.

immersePlan.name: Say hotep to someone
immersePlan.text: Hotep means peace, offering, satisfied. Say it, or the idea of it, to someone today. Wish them peace, and see how it sounds in your own mouth.

immersePlan.name: Write in medu netjer
immersePlan.text: Medu netjer means the words of the god, the hieroglyphs. Write your name in hieroglyphs using an online chart, and put it in a cartouche. Draw it slowly.

rules.text: Tell the truth, even in small things
rules.why: Maat is truth. The Instructions repeat that honest speech is the foundation of a good life.

rules.text: Do not take what is not yours
rules.why: The scribes taught that moving a boundary stone or falsifying a weight was among the gravest offences. Be exact about what is yours.

rules.text: Feed the hungry and clothe the bare
rules.why: Tomb inscriptions list gifts of bread, water and clothing as evidence of a good life. Give something real to someone today.
The declaration of innocence includes “I have not made anyone weep”. Notice who might be hurt by what you do.

rules.text: Speak the names of the dead
rules.why: The Egyptians held that a person lives on while their name is spoken. Remember someone in this way.
Egyptian scribes valued precision. Measure, count and write carefully, and let the small numbers be right.

read.title: Ancient Egyptian Literature
read.creator: Miriam Lichtheim
read.why: Three volumes of translated Egyptian texts, from Pyramid Texts to tales and wisdom writings.

read.title: The Egyptian Book of the Dead: The Book of Going Forth by Day
read.creator: Translated by Raymond Faulkner, edited by Ogden Goelet
read.why: A beautifully illustrated translation of the papyrus of Ani with commentary.

read.title: The Rise and Fall of Ancient Egypt
read.creator: Toby Wilkinson
read.why: A narrative history from the first kings to Cleopatra.

read.title: The Complete Gods and Goddesses of Ancient Egypt
read.creator: Richard H. Wilkinson
read.why: A well-illustrated guide to the deities and their meanings.

read.title: The Mind of Egypt
read.creator: Jan Assmann
read.why: A scholar of religion considers the ideas and mentality of Egyptian civilisation.

read.title: The Story of Sinuhe
read.creator: Anonymous, in Lichtheim’s Ancient Egyptian Literature
read.why: A tale of an exile who longs for home, and one of the oldest stories in the world.

read.title: Sinuhe the Egyptian
read.creator: Mika Waltari
read.why: A novel by a Finnish writer, set in the age of Akhenaten. Fiction, but an enduring one.

watch.title: Egypt’s Golden Empire
watch.creator: PBS, directed by Mike Beckham and Jeff Duncan
watch.why: A documentary on the New Kingdom, from Hatshepsut to Ramesses II.

watch.title: Secrets of Lost Empires: Obelisk
watch.creator: NOVA
watch.why: A team raises a real obelisk with ancient methods to learn how the Egyptians did it.

watch.title: Cleopatra
watch.creator: Joseph L. Mankiewicz
watch.why: The long, lavish Hollywood epic of the last queen of Egypt, with Elizabeth Taylor. It is entertaining and often far from history, and it began a century of Egyptomania.

listen.title: Aida
listen.creator: Giuseppe Verdi
listen.why: An opera set in ancient Egypt, premiered in Cairo. The music is an outsider’s dream of the Nile.

listen.title: Escalay: The Water Wheel
listen.creator: Hamza El Din
listen.why: The oud of a Nubian master, from the Nile’s south.

listen.title: Enta Omri
listen.creator: Umm Kulthum
listen.why: The great Egyptian singer in a long song composed by Mohamed Abdel Wahab. A modern classic of the Arab world.

art.title: The Great Sphinx of Giza
art.creator: Old Kingdom builders
art.why: A lion with a human head, carved from bedrock. Probably an image of the king Khafre.

art.title: The bust of Nefertiti
art.creator: Thutmose
art.why: Painted limestone, found in 1912 and kept in the Neues Museum in Berlin.

art.title: The funerary mask of Tutankhamun
art.creator: Royal craftsmen
art.why: Gold and lapis, found in 1922. In the Egyptian Museum in Cairo.

art.title: The Book of the Dead of Hunefer
art.creator: Scribe Hunefer
art.why: A painted papyrus with a famous scene of the weighing of the heart, in the British Museum.

art.title: The tomb of Nefertari
art.creator: Painters of the Valley of the Queens
art.why: Brilliant wall paintings in the tomb of Ramesses II’s queen.

eat.title: Bread
eat.creator: Emmer wheat, as the ancient Egyptians ate
eat.why: The staple. Loaves were baked in many shapes, and bread was used in offerings.

eat.title: Onions and garlic
eat.creator: Raw or in a salad
eat.why: Common to workers and kings. Onions appear on offering tables.

eat.title: Lentil soup
eat.creator: Plain, with olive oil
eat.why: Lentils were a staple of the ancient diet and of modern Egypt.

eat.title: Dates and figs
eat.creator: A handful
eat.why: Sweet fruits eaten fresh and dried, and used in baking.

eat.title: Ful medames
eat.creator: Slow-cooked fava beans with oil and lemon
eat.why: A national dish of modern Egypt, eaten at breakfast.

eat.title: Ta’amiya
eat.creator: Fava bean fritters, with herbs
eat.why: The Egyptian version of falafel. A street food of modern Egypt.

drink.title: Karkade
drink.creator: Hibiscus tea, hot or cold
drink.why: A deep red drink that is a favourite across Egypt and the Sudan.

drink.title: Mint tea
drink.creator: Black or green tea with fresh mint
drink.why: A drink of hospitality in modern Egypt.

drink.title: Barley water
drink.creator: Boiled barley, cooled and strained
drink.why: Barley was the grain of ancient beer. This is a plain, non-alcoholic cousin.

customs.title: Say the name
customs.creator: Speak the name of someone who has died
customs.why: The Egyptians held that a person lives while the name is said.

customs.title: Offer bread and water
customs.creator: Share a simple gift of food and drink
customs.why: The "offering formula" asked for thousands of loaves and jars of beer for the dead.

customs.title: Wash before the day’s work
customs.creator: A deliberate wash with attention
customs.why: Priests washed before entering the temple, and cleanliness was a mark of order.

customs.title: Keep three seasons
customs.creator: Mark the flood, the sowing and the harvest in your own calendar
customs.why: Shape your year in three parts.

customs.title: Write a name with care
customs.creator: A hieroglyph or a plain letter
customs.why: The Egyptians wrote names in rings of protection. Take care with names.

games.title: Senet
games.creator: Board game · Egypt
games.why: Thirty squares in three rows. Later Egyptians read it as the soul’s passage through the underworld, and four sets were found in Tutankhamun’s tomb.

games.title: Mehen
games.creator: Board game · Egypt
games.why: A round board in the form of a coiled snake, played with lion pieces and marbles. The rules are lost.

games.title: Hounds and Jackals
games.creator: Board game · Egypt
games.why: A race of ten pegs round a palm tree. A fine ivory set from Thebes is in the Metropolitan Museum.

games.title: Assassin’s Creed Origins: Discovery Tour
games.creator: Video game · Ubisoft Montreal
games.why: A combat-free walk through Ptolemaic Egypt with tours written with Egyptologists: mummification, the Library of Alexandria, daily life on the Nile.

games.title: Pharaoh: A New Era
games.creator: Video game · Triskell Interactive
games.why: A remake of the 1999 city builder. Raise a town on the Nile, manage the flood and build your way up to pyramids.

festivals.title: Wepet Renpet
festivals.creator: Midsummer, at the rising of Sirius
festivals.why: The opening of the year, when the star Sirius returned to the dawn sky and the Nile began to rise.

festivals.title: Opet Festival
festivals.creator: Second month of the flood season, Thebes
festivals.why: The statues of Amun, Mut and Khonsu travelled from Karnak to Luxor Temple amid crowds, music and free bread and beer.

festivals.title: Beautiful Festival of the Valley
festivals.creator: Early summer, Thebes
festivals.why: Amun crossed the river to the west bank, and families ate and drank through the night at the tombs of their dead.

festivals.title: Sham el-Nessim
festivals.creator: The Monday after Coptic Easter, Egypt
festivals.why: A spring picnic day kept by Egyptians of every faith, with salted fish, onions and coloured eggs. Many trace it to pharaonic times.

festivals.title: Sun festival at Abu Simbel
festivals.creator: About 22 February and 22 October
festivals.why: At dawn the sun reaches down the temple axis and lights the statues in the inner sanctuary.

places.title: Giza
places.creator: Greater Cairo, Egypt
places.why: The three great pyramids and the Sphinx, with the workers’ town to the south.

places.title: Grand Egyptian Museum
places.creator: Giza, Egypt
places.why: Opened in full in 2025 beside the pyramids, with the complete contents of Tutankhamun’s tomb shown together for the first time.

places.title: Karnak
places.creator: Luxor, Egypt
places.why: Two thousand years of building for Amun. Stand among the 134 columns of the great hall.

places.title: Valley of the Kings
places.creator: West bank, Luxor, Egypt
places.why: Painted royal tombs of the New Kingdom, their walls covered with the books of the afterlife.

places.title: Deir el-Medina
places.creator: West bank, Luxor, Egypt
places.why: The village of the tomb builders, with their houses, chapels and own small, bright tombs.

places.title: Abydos
places.creator: Sohag Governorate, Egypt
places.why: The temple of Seti I, with the finest reliefs in Egypt, at the old cult centre of Osiris.

places.title: Saqqara
places.creator: South of Cairo, Egypt
places.why: The Step Pyramid of Djoser, the first great building in stone, designed by Imhotep.

ethics.title: Speak truth
ethics.text: The Instructions and tomb inscriptions treat honest speech as the basis of social life. The ideal is plain, steady speech.
ethics.practice: Speak one thing plainly today where you might have been vague.

ethics.title: Give bread to the hungry
ethics.text: A great number of tomb autobiographies claim that the owner gave bread to the hungry, clothes to the naked and a boat to the stranded. Generosity was the proof of a righteous life.
ethics.practice: Give food or money to someone who needs it, without being asked.

ethics.title: Humility before knowledge
ethics.text: Ptahhotep advises not to be proud of knowledge and to consult both ignorant and wise, because mastery of a craft is never complete.
ethics.practice: Ask someone you think knows less than you for their view.

ethics.title: Fairness in measure
ethics.text: Amenemope warns against moving boundary markers and falsifying scales. Honest weights are a sign of an honest heart.
ethics.practice: Look for a place where you rounded in your own favour and correct it.

ethics.title: Protect the weak
ethics.text: The Eloquent Peasant, a Middle Kingdom story, shows a poor man demanding justice from an official. Justice must reach the lowest.
ethics.practice: Defend someone who has little power, even in a small way.

ethics.title: Keep your composure
ethics.text: Amenemope contrasts the heated man with the truly silent one, who is like a tree growing quietly in a garden.
ethics.practice: Wait ten seconds before your next heated reply.

philosophy.title: Maat
philosophy.text: Maat means truth, justice, balance and cosmic order, and also names the goddess who stands for them. To the Egyptians the world was held in order by acts that agreed with Maat, and disorder, isfet, was always at the edge.
philosophy.practice: Name one thing that restores balance in a situation you face today.

philosophy.title: The parts of a person
philosophy.text: A person was made of several parts: the body, the name, the shadow, the heart, the ka and the ba. After death these had to be reunited and nourished for the person to live again. The self was plural.
philosophy.practice: List four parts of your own self: body, name, habits, and what you leave behind.

philosophy.title: The sun’s journey
philosophy.text: Each night the sun god Ra travelled through the Duat, the underworld, and each dawn he was reborn. The cycle gave a model of death and renewal for every person.
philosophy.practice: Think of an ending in your life as a night journey before a morning.

philosophy.title: The weighing of the heart
philosophy.text: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat. A heavy heart, burdened by wrongdoing, would be devoured by the monster Ammit. The image makes conscience visible.
philosophy.practice: Ask what would make your heart heavier or lighter tomorrow.

philosophy.title: Heka
philosophy.text: Heka, often translated as magic, was the power of words and acts to shape reality. Gods themselves used it. In daily life it was carried out through spells, amulets and recitations that were believed to work.
philosophy.practice: Say one sentence today that you intend to make true.

philosophy.title: The name
philosophy.text: A person’s name was a part of their being. Erasing a name from a monument was meant to destroy them, and speaking it kept them alive.
philosophy.practice: Write the full name of someone you love and think of its meaning.

philosophy.title: Memory as immortality
philosophy.text: The Egyptians built tombs, statues and written lives to keep memory alive. To be remembered and spoken of was a kind of eternity.
philosophy.practice: Write three sentences you would want someone to say about you.

philosophy.title: The Nile cycle
philosophy.text: The yearly flood brought new soil and the promise of harvest. Egyptians accepted the cycle of flood, growth and harvest as the pattern of life.
philosophy.practice: Identify your own cycle of rest, effort and harvest.

philosophy.title: One god or many
philosophy.text: Akhenaten promoted the Aten, the sun disc, above all other gods in the fourteenth century BCE. His Great Hymn praises a single giver of life. Whether it was monotheism or something else is still debated.
philosophy.practice: Read a few lines of the Great Hymn to the Aten and notice what it praises.

philosophy.title: The first time
philosophy.text: Egyptian creation stories describe a mound arising from the waters of chaos, with a creator who spoke or thought the world into being. Different cities told different versions.
philosophy.practice: Think of how a piece of work of yours began from a mound in a mess.

What do you hope to be remembered for?
What would you put in a tomb or letter to the future?
What did you learn about humility?
Whom did you listen to?
What is your heart heavy with?
What is light in your heart?
What would you ask a wise elder?

Where did you see something beautiful that will last?

What changed when you weighed your heart each evening?
Whose name did you speak, and what did it bring up?
What did the seasons teach you about timing?
What will you keep: the morning, the sign, the weighing or the season?
What would you like to learn about Egypt from Egyptian scholars?

intro: Ancient Egyptian civilisation grew along the Nile for more than three thousand years. Its kings ruled from about 3100 BCE, when tradition says Narmer joined the upper and lower lands, until the last Greek and Roman rulers. In that time it built pyramids and temples, invented a system of writing, kept records on papyrus, and developed laws, medicine, mathematics, and a rich religious and ethical thought.

The river shaped everything. Every year the Nile flooded and left rich black silt, and Egyptians named their country Kemet, the black land, against the red land of the desert. Their calendar had three seasons of four months: the flood, the growing season and the harvest. The sun that crossed the sky and was reborn each dawn, and the river that returned every year, taught them a world of cycles.

Their central ethical idea was Maat: truth, justice, balance and the order of the universe. Kings were responsible for maintaining it, and every person could contribute through honest speech and fair dealing. Against Maat stood isfet, disorder and falsehood. In the afterlife, the heart of the dead was weighed against the feather of Maat, and the person who had lived justly could pass to eternal life.

Egyptian wisdom literature, the Instructions of Ptahhotep and Amenemope among others, gives practical advice about speech, restraint, honesty and generosity. Tomb inscriptions record the good that people claimed to have done, such as giving bread to the hungry. The picture of the Egyptians as obsessed only with death is misleading: the tomb was a way of keeping life going, and the surviving texts show warmth, humour and love of this world.

We know them through monuments, tombs and papyri, and the story of how we learned to read them is itself remarkable. After the last hieroglyphic inscription was carved in 394 CE, the script fell out of use. The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, held the same text in hieroglyphs, a later script and Greek, and in 1822 Jean-François Champollion announced that he had deciphered it. Howard Carter’s discovery of Tutankhamun’s tomb in 1922 made Egypt famous again.

This Onda borrows a few habits from that world: a morning of truth, a hieroglyph, an evening weighing of the heart and a sense of season. It is not a religion and does not ask you to worship its gods. Modern books and films also carry many invented claims about Egypt, from lost advanced technology to alien builders, which the evidence does not support. The Egyptians built their monuments themselves, with skill and organisation.
guide.origin: The Nile valley and delta in north-east Africa

figures.name: Imhotep
figures.bio: Official and architect under King Djoser, credited with the Step Pyramid at Saqqara. Later honoured as a god of healing.

figures.name: Hatshepsut
figures.bio: Became pharaoh after the death of her husband and ruled for about two decades. She built a great temple at Deir el-Bahari and sent a trading expedition to Punt.

figures.name: Akhenaten
figures.bio: King who promoted the worship of the sun disc, the Aten, moved the capital to Amarna and changed Egyptian art.

figures.name: Nefertiti
figures.bio: Queen and wife of Akhenaten. Her painted bust is among the most famous works of ancient art.

figures.name: Tutankhamun
figures.bio: A boy king whose nearly intact tomb was found in 1922. He restored the old gods after Akhenaten.

figures.name: Ramesses II
figures.bio: Long-reigning king who built Abu Simbel and signed an early peace treaty with the Hittites.

figures.name: Ptahhotep
figures.bio: Official credited with an Instruction of advice to his son. The surviving texts are copies made centuries later.

figures.name: Cleopatra VII
figures.bio: The last active ruler of Ptolemaic Egypt. Spoke Egyptian and Greek, and died after the defeat of Antony and her at Actium.

figures.name: Jean-François Champollion
figures.bio: French scholar who announced the decipherment of hieroglyphs in 1822.

figures.name: Howard Carter
figures.bio: English archaeologist who found Tutankhamun’s tomb in November 1922 after years of searching.

history.detail: Tradition credits King Narmer, or Menes, with joining Upper and Lower Egypt. The Narmer Palette shows a king wearing the crowns of both lands.
Djoser’s architect, traditionally Imhotep, built the first monumental stone structure at Saqqara by stacking mastabas on top of each other.
Khufu’s pyramid at Giza, about 146 metres tall when finished, was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly four thousand years.
After a period of division, Mentuhotep II reunited Egypt and began a classical age of literature, art and administration.
Rulers from the Levant held the north of Egypt for about a century. Theban kings expelled them and began the New Kingdom under Ahmose.
Acting first as regent, she took the royal titles and ruled for about twenty years, building monuments and sending a trading mission to Punt.
Akhenaten promoted the Aten, built a new capital at Amarna and changed art and religion. After his death the old order returned.
A long reign of monuments, battles and diplomacy, including the treaty with the Hittites after the Battle of Kadesh.
Alexander the Great took Egypt from the Persians and was welcomed. After his death, the Ptolemies, a dynasty founded by one of his generals, ruled for nearly three centuries from Alexandria.
After the defeat of Antony and Cleopatra the country became a province of Rome, and a granary of the empire.
The last datable hieroglyphic inscription was carved at the temple of Philae on 24 August 394. The ability to read the script was soon lost.

history.what: The Rosetta Stone and its decipherment
history.detail: French soldiers found the stone in 1799. In 1822 Champollion showed that hieroglyphs were partly sound signs and partly sense signs, and that they recorded the Egyptian language.
On 4 November Howard Carter’s team found the first step to the tomb in the Valley of the Kings. The contents, almost untouched, took years to catalogue.

concepts.text: Truth, justice, balance and cosmic order.
concepts.detail: The central value of Egyptian thought. It was both an abstract principle and a goddess with a feather headdress. Kings were said to "live by Maat" and offer it to the gods. Ordinary people sought it in honest speech and just dealing.

The ka was a life force sustained by offerings, the ba a free-moving personality shown as a human-headed bird, and the akh the transfigured spirit that succeeded in the afterlife. They had to be united after death for a person to live on.

In the Book of the Dead, spell 125, the heart is weighed against the feather of Maat while Thoth records the result. The deceased recites a list of denials, such as "I have not stolen". If the heart is light, they proceed to Osiris. If not, the monster Ammit devours it.

concepts.text: The underworld the sun travels at night.
concepts.detail: The sun god Ra sailed through twelve hours of night, fighting the serpent Apophis, and was reborn at dawn. The dead hoped to join the voyage. It is both a map of the afterlife and a metaphor for renewal.

concepts.text: The power of effective words and acts.
concepts.detail: A force that existed before the gods and was used by them. Spells, amulets and rituals tapped it. It was not set apart from medicine and craft, and physicians used both remedies and spells.
To speak or write a name kept its owner alive, and to erase it destroyed them. Kings placed theirs in cartouches, and tomb walls repeat names so that visitors would read them aloud.

concepts.text: The king as the link between gods and people.
concepts.detail: The king was Horus alive on earth and the son of Ra, responsible for maintaining Maat by building temples, giving offerings and defending the land. Many kings were weak, and the ideal was tested often.

The script mixes signs for sounds, signs for whole words and silent determinatives that show the kind of word. There are 24 single-consonant signs. It could be written in rows or columns, and the signs face the beginning of the line.
Scribes copied texts of advice, such as those of Ptahhotep, Merikare and Amenemope. They teach restraint in speech, fairness, kindness to the poor and humility. They were used to train young scribes.

Akhet, peret and shemu shaped the year. The flood arrived in summer, the sowing and growth followed in the cooler months, and the harvest came in spring. Temple festivals and work followed the same rhythm.

facts.text: The pyramids were built by organised crews of Egyptian workers, who were housed, fed and buried near the pyramids at Giza. They were not slaves.
Cleopatra VII lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid.
The Edwin Smith Papyrus, from about 1600 BCE, describes 48 medical cases in a systematic way, with examination, diagnosis and treatment.
Egyptians played senet, a board game, and several sets were buried with Tutankhamun.
The hieroglyphic alphabet of single-consonant signs has about 24 signs, but the script as a whole used hundreds of signs.
The Great Pyramid held the record as the tallest structure in the world for more than 3,800 years, until the spire of Lincoln Cathedral was completed around 1311.
Abu Simbel’s temples were cut into pieces and moved to higher ground in the 1960s to save them from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

sensitivity.note: Ancient Egyptian religion is no longer practised as a continuous tradition, though some modern groups reconstruct it. This Onda borrows ethical ideas, habits of attention and cultural material, and does not ask you to worship its gods. Vowels in Egyptian words are conventional, since the script did not record them.
requiredCaveats: Pronunciations are modern conventions used by Egyptologists. Nobody knows exactly how the words sounded.
Be wary of popular claims about pyramid power, lost technology or alien builders. The evidence shows that the Egyptians built their monuments themselves.
Modern Egyptians are the people of today’s Egypt, not a museum. Learn from Egyptian scholars, writers and artists as well as from foreign Egyptologists.
